name: Idrisid and Aghlabid states
summary: The first Islamic dynasties to rule North Africa apart from the caliphs: the Idrisids, who founded Fez, and the Aghlabids of Tunisia, who conquered Sicily; both were swept away by the Fatimids.

location.value: North Africa: the Idrisids ruled northern Morocco; the Aghlabids ruled Ifriqiya (Tunisia, eastern Algeria and Tripolitania).

terrain.value: Mediterranean coasts and plains, the Atlas and Rif mountains, and the edge of the Sahara.

climate.value: Mediterranean on the coast, with dry summers; drier inland towards the Sahara.

resources.value: Grain, olives and dates; Saharan trade routes bringing gold from West Africa.

population.value: Perhaps a few million, mostly Berber farmers and herders.

urbanisation.value: Fez (founded 789, enlarged by Idris II) and Kairouan were large cities; the Aghlabids built palace towns at al-Abbasiyya and Raqqada.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Arab settlers, and refugees from al-Andalus and Kairouan who settled in Fez.

economicBase.value: Farming, with irrigation and large reservoirs at Kairouan, plus Mediterranean and Saharan trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Mediterranean sea trade and caravan routes across the Sahara through Sijilmasa.

wealth.value: Kairouan grew rich under the Aghlabids; the Idrisids were less wealthy.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver dirhams (Idrisids) and gold dinars (Aghlabids); land taxes and taxes on non-Muslims.

inequality.value: An Arab ruling elite above Berber farmers; slaves served in the Aghlabid army.

governmentType.value: Two dynasties of emirs: the Idrisids (788–974) and the Aghlabids (800–909), who ruled for the Abbasid caliphs in name.

keyRulers.value: Idris I and Idris II (Idrisids); Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab and Ziyadat Allah I (Aghlabids).

succession.value: Hereditary within each dynasty; the Aghlabid emir needed the caliph’s formal approval.

institutions.value: Emirs’ courts, judges (qadis) following Maliki law, and great mosques as centres of learning.

stability.value: After Idris II died (828), Idrisid lands were split among his sons and weakened.

eliteConflict.value: Rival heirs among the Idrisids; army revolts against the Aghlabid emirs.

armyAndTech.value: The Aghlabids had a strong navy and coastal forts (ribats) such as Sousse and Monastir.

majorWars.value: The Aghlabid conquest of Sicily from the Byzantines (827–902), from Mazara to Taormina.

territoryChange.value: The Aghlabids gained Sicily (827–902) and Malta (870).

alliancesRivals.value: Aghlabids loyal to the Abbasids; Idrisids independent.

inventions.value: No major inventions; the Aghlabid reservoirs of Kairouan were impressive water engineering.

scienceEducation.value: The Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez (founded 857 by Fatima al-Fihri) and the Great Mosque of Kairouan were centres of learning.

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Roads, caravan routes and coastal shipping.

languageWriting.value: Arabic for government and religion; Berber languages spoken by most people.

artsArchitecture.value: The Great Mosque of Kairouan (rebuilt in 836), the Great Mosque of Sousse and the ribats; early Islamic Fez.

socialStructure.value: Arabs, Berbers, Andalusi settlers, Jewish and Christian communities, and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the ruler and to Islam, alongside Berber tribal identities.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

neighbours.value: The Umayyads of Córdoba, the Rustamids of Tahert, the Abbasid Caliphate and the Byzantine Empire.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Sunni Islam among the Berbers; Kairouan became a centre of Maliki law.

colonisation.value: The Aghlabids conquered Byzantine Sicily and settled Muslims there.

riseSignals.value: Idris I, a descendant of the Prophet fleeing the Abbasids, was welcomed by Berbers at Walili (788).

peakPeriod.value: The 800s: Aghlabid Kairouan and the conquest of Sicily; the founding of Fez and the Qarawiyyin.

declineSignals.value: The Fatimids, backed by the Kutama Berbers, overthrew the Aghlabids (909).

outcome.value: The Aghlabids fell to the Fatimids (909); the last Idrisids were defeated by the Umayyads of Córdoba (974).

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
